Revised assessment using the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey (SLOOS): The FOMC statement notes modest growth, robust job gains, low unemployment, and elevated inflation while holding the policy rate at 5 to 5-1/4 percent and continuing balance sheet reduction. The Committee also flags that tighter credit conditions will weigh on activity, hiring, and inflation.

The April 2023 SLOOS substantiates and amplifies this headwind. Banks reported broad-based tightening of standards and terms across C&I and commercial real estate loans (including wider spreads, lower loan-to-value ratios, and higher debt service coverage ratios) and across consumer credit (credit cards, autos, HELOCs, subprime, and other consumer loans). Reasons cited included a weaker economic outlook, deteriorating collateral values, higher funding costs, deposit outflows, and liquidity concerns; many banks also raised credit scoring thresholds. Loan demand weakened across business uses (plant/equipment, M&A, inventory, and A/R financing), and banks—domestic and foreign—expect further tightening ahead, with foreign banks also indicating tighter spreads and plans to tighten C&I. While there were pockets of nuance (e.g., some mid-sized banks eased GSE-eligible mortgage standards; largest banks tightened credit cards on credit quality), the net picture is a clear, ongoing tightening impulse.

Taken together, the SLOOS corroborates the FOMC’s caution and suggests tighter credit will more meaningfully restrain growth than the labor data alone implies. This tempers the earlier mildly positive tone to a slightly cautious one.
